newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Clashes marr start of Bangui mediator's peace bid.
newsitem.headline: Clashes marr start of Bangui mediator's peace bid.

text.p: Fresh fighting broke out in the Central African Republic capital Bangui on Thursday as newly returned Malian mediator Amadou Toumani Toure began talks to try to broker a ceasefire, witnesses said.
The MISAB African peacekeeping force and disaffected soldiers blamed one another for starting the clashes, during which the two sides exchanged automatic arms fire.
"The MISAB gives us no guarantee of security," Lieutenant Parfait Mabay, spokesman for the dissident soldiers, told Reuters. "They hunt down the ex-mutineers to kill them."
He accused peacekeepers of starting the violence to derail the peace talks. A MISAB spokesman accused the dissident soldiers of starting the fighting.

Toumani Toure, Mali's widely respected former military leader, brokered a January 25 peace deal to end three army mutinies in under a year. Officials said he launched his latest talks with a meeting of the follow-up committee he presides.
Clashes broke out on June 20 after an incident involving peacekeepers and a group of soldiers who had yet to rejoin their units under the January deal.

Red Cross officials say the clashes have killed at least 80 people, many of them civilians. Thousands of civilians have fled the southern suburbs, stronghold of the dissident soldiers and focus of the fighting.

Former colonial power France, which has troops in the country under a defence pact, intervened in support of the peacekeepers and one of its helicopters hit mortar batteries manned by dissident soldiers after its embassy came under fire.
Five French nationals in the embassy compound were among scores of people injured in the fighting.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 in Bangui began as pay protests but evolved into a bid to topple President Ange-Felix Patasse, a civilian from the north, elected in 1993. A third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
French troops intervened directly to stop the fighting before handing over to the African peacekeeping force.
Toumani Toure returned to Bangui on Wednesday.
"It's the fourth time I'm coming here to the Central African Republic. I hope it's the last time that I come to sort out this problem of mutiny," he told reporters at Bangui airport.

Toumani Toure, who steered his West African country to democracy in 1992 after toppling dictator Moussa Traore, has repeatedly said Central African Republic citizens must solve the problem amongst themselves and no-one can do it for them.
Over 300 marchers supporting the disaffected soldiers, some carrying bodies, marched to the French embassy on Wednesday to accuse France and the peacekeepers of siding with Patasse.
Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo have troops in the 800-strong force. Patasse opponents criticise the Chadians, saying Patasse hired Chadians in a private militia.
The local Red Cross said it had been swamped by tens of thousands of people who fled the southern districts after peacekeepers fired shells from tanks and heavy mortars.

"There is not enough drinking water, there is not enough food," Dr David Dofara, head of the local Red Cross, told Reuters. He said the number of people displaced by fighting rose to over 40,000 on Wednesday from around 8,000 before.
Germany said it was closing its Bangui embassy temporarily.
